newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba seen holding rates, but reserves move possible.
newsitem.headline: Buba seen holding rates, but reserves move possible.

text.p: The policy-making council of the German central bank began its regular meeting on Thursday with most economists predicting interest rates would be held steady, but there was speculation its reserves policy could change.

Economists polled by Reuters this week predicted the Bundesbank would leave its three main interest rates, the discount, Lombard and repurchase (repo) rates, unchanged because there were no compelling reasons to shift policy at this moment.
In addition, they expected the main money market rate, the repo, to be kept steady at three percent for the next several weeks. This rate has been at three percent since late August.
The Bundesbank last cut its discount and Lombard rates in April, when the discount rate fell to 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate to 4.50 percent.

Although soft October industrial output data fanned speculation that the Bundesbank could be tempted to nudge rates lower to boost economic growth, the Bundesbank recently reiterated that it sees no need to adjust rates now.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer is chairing the meeting, the Bundesbank said in answer to enquiries. No outside guests will be in attendance.

However, speculation has grown that the Bundesbank might announce a decision today to exempt securities repurchase agreements from minimum reserve requirements, as part of ongoing efforts to improve Germany's standing as a financial centre.
In repurchase agreements, a party borrows short-term funds by selling securities with a promise to buy them back at a later date. The difference betweem the prices represents the interest.

Banks in Germany currently have to deposit a certain percentage of short-term borrowings from foreign banks and domestic non-banks in non-interest bearing Bundesbank deposits. The current level on repurchase agreements and sight deposits is two percent. Savings depsoits require 1.5 percent.
The minimum reserve requirement is widely seen as a burden, which has prompted banks to shift their repurchase business in German securities from Frankfurt to London.

The Bundesbank is the only central bank among industrialised European nations that requires banks to hold reserves in non-interest bearing accounts and is lobbying hard for the future European Central Bank to adopt the concept.
But if the Bundesbank takes such a step, it would not mean Germany will abandon its concept of holding minimum reserves, which it deems as an important measure to guide monetary policy.
